specAnchors.text: describe how a chain reaction can be set up if the neutrons produced by one fission strike other U-235 nuclei
describe the role played by the control rods and moderator in the fission process
understand the role of shielding around a nuclear reactor

primer.text: A reactor is fission kept on a leash: neutrons from each split find fresh U-235 nuclei and the chain keeps turning, control rods meter how many neutrons survive, the moderator slows them to the speed that splits uranium efficiently, and thick steel-and-concrete shielding soaks up the radiation so workers outside stay safe.

modules.title: Chain reactions
modules.opening: One neutron induces a fission, and that fission releases two or three neutrons — each free to strike another U-235 nucleus and split it in turn. That self-feeding sequence is a chain reaction, and if the fissile material exceeds its critical mass the reaction accelerates into an uncontrolled release.
keyPoints: Neutrons from one fission can strike other U-235 nuclei and trigger more fissions.
A chain reaction continues because each split hands neutrons on to the next generation.
One induced fission needs a single neutron but releases two or three.
Above the critical mass of fissile material the reaction rate accelerates uncontrollably.

low.restatement: One neutron in, two-or-three out: the surplus neutrons feed the next splits.
low.analogy: Popcorn popping: each bursting kernel flicks others hot enough to burst, and the pan goes from one pop to many in seconds.
low.examPointer: Chain-reaction diagrams want neutrons drawn striking further U-235 nuclei — clarity beats artwork.

medium.restatement: The neutron census grows 1 → 2–3 → 4–9 → …, so above the critical mass the fission rate compounds without bound.
medium.analogy: A rumour where every listener retells it to two friends — the audience doubles each round until the whole school has heard it.
medium.examPointer: Generation-counting questions are just powers of two — write the sequence out rather than jumping to the answer.

modules.title: Control rods and the moderator
modules.opening: A running reactor must hold both the number of free neutrons and their energy in check. Control rods made of neutron-absorbing material are lowered or raised to set the fission rate, while the moderator slows fast neutrons into thermal neutrons that react efficiently with the uranium fuel; in normal running exactly one neutron from each fission goes on to cause the next.
keyPoints: Control rods absorb neutrons so the chain reaction runs at a steady, chosen rate.
Lowering the rods absorbs more neutrons and slows fission; raising them lets fission speed up.
The moderator slows fast neutrons into thermal neutrons that split uranium efficiently.
In normal running, exactly one neutron from each fission causes the next fission.
For an emergency shutdown the rods drop fully in and the reactions stop.

low.restatement: Rods ration the neutrons; the moderator slows them so each one counts.
low.analogy: A turnstile and a walking pace: the rods admit only so many visitors per minute, and the moderator makes sure each walks slowly enough to buy a ticket.
low.examPointer: Two-component questions want both roles named — rods absorb, moderator slows. Mixing them loses the marks.

medium.restatement: Steady power means one neutron per fission seeds the next; rods trim the surplus and the moderator tunes the speed for efficient capture.
medium.analogy: Cruise control: the rods are the brake pedal, the moderator the gear that keeps the engine in its efficient band.
medium.examPointer: Shutdown = rods fully in; rate-up = rods raised; rate-down = rods lowered. Learn the three rod positions.

modules.title: Shielding the reactor
modules.opening: Everything that leaves a fission is hazardous: the daughter nuclei and the emitted neutrons are radioactive. So the entire reactor is wrapped in shielding — a steel and concrete wall nearly two metres thick that absorbs the emissions and keeps the environment around the reactor safe for workers.
keyPoints: Shielding surrounds the whole reactor and absorbs its hazardous radiation.
The daughter nuclei formed in fission, and the neutrons emitted, are radioactive.
A steel and concrete wall close to two metres thick keeps the surroundings safe for workers.

low.restatement: Thick steel and concrete soak up the reactor's radiation so nobody outside is exposed.
low.analogy: A lead-lined apron at the dentist, scaled up to a wall that wraps the whole machine.
low.examPointer: Quote the thickness as 'nearly two metres' and the materials as steel and concrete — both attract marks.

medium.restatement: Fission products stay radioactive after the split, so the absorbing wall is the last line between the core and the workforce.
medium.analogy: A soundproofed rehearsal room: the noise (radiation) stays inside because the walls (steel and concrete) absorb it before it reaches the corridor.
medium.examPointer: Tie shielding to the radioactivity of daughters and neutrons — the causal chain earns the explanation mark.

glossary.definition: A self-feeding sequence in which neutrons from each fission trigger further fissions.
The minimum amount of fissile material needed to sustain a chain reaction.
Neutron-absorbing rods whose depth in the core sets the fission rate.
Material that slows fast neutrons into thermal neutrons that split uranium efficiently.
Steel-and-concrete wall, nearly two metres thick, that absorbs the reactor's hazardous radiation.

workedExample.prompt: Complete the chain-reaction diagram for uranium-235: how does the drawing show the reaction spreading?
steps: Draw the released neutrons striking further U-235 nuclei — it is the neutron strikes that cause the next fissions.
Show each struck nucleus splitting and releasing two or more neutrons of its own.
With each generation the neutron count rises, so more and more fissions follow.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The chain spreads generation by generation: each fission needs one neutron and releases two or more, so the number of reactions keeps growing.
